Today, we commence the first session of CSCEC8B Overseas Design Standards Training Series in an online format—the specialized training on U.S. standards for electrical design. This training is both a concrete action to implement the bureau’s overseas business strategy and a critical initiative to address gaps in overseas design capabilities and build a robust design support system.

First, on behalf of the Design Management Academy, I extend a warm welcome to all colleagues who have overcome time zone differences to attend this training. A special thanks to our instructor, Professor Fan Ziyu, joining us from Canada. Professor Fan is a registered electrical engineer in multiple Canadian provinces, a Tsinghua University graduate, and brings extensive experience from both Chinese design institutes and North American engineering projects. Despite the time zone challenge, Professor Fan will teach daily from 6 PM to 11 PM (local time). We deeply appreciate his dedication.

Today’s participants are all key members of CSCEC8B’s overseas design teams, including MEP chief engineers from Southeast Asia and North Africa regions, senior electrical designers, and young talents newly joining the overseas division. You all understand the decisive impact of local-standard-compliant drawings and precise detailed designs on project cost, schedule, and quality—as well as the importance of effective communication with overseas clients and consultants.

Last month, the bureau officially issued the Implementation Plan for CSCEC8B’s Overseas Design Management Mechanism and System Development, aiming to address issues such as weak design philosophy, insufficient collaboration, and capability gaps in overseas projects. The plan establishes a management model of “strong headquarters support and robust project execution,” emphasizing design as the cornerstone of overseas project management. Through standardization, resource integration, and talent development, the plan seeks to transform design from a backend support role to a frontend driver, fostering deeper collaboration among design, procurement, and construction.

Recently, the Academy has collected thousands of overseas design standards from over 20 countries, covering U.S., British, and Southeast Asian/North African local standards. These will be systematically categorized and uploaded to the CSCEC8B Cloud Platform. This training is a pivotal step in implementing the plan, advancing in parallel with the standards database development.

Next, I will introduce the organizations responsible for developing these codes and standards in North America, and list the currently applied codes, standards, and regulations.

Then, we will discuss the specific methods for applying these codes and standards, as well as coordination with the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) and inspection agencies.

说话人3: 00:12:18 - 00:15:25

Everyone should pay attention to the importance of electrical codes and standards application. When carrying out construction projects abroad, it is usually necessary to apply for construction permits such as Building Permit or Development Permit, as well as Electrical Permit (electrical construction permit). Upon completion of construction, the project must also pass inspection by the relevant authorities. These processes are directly related to codes and standards. If the design or construction fails to comply with code requirements, the project will be rejected during inspection.

Following codes in design and construction can avoid future claims or at least minimize them. This is because overseas, if accidents occur due to design or construction issues, the owner has the right to file lawsuits for compensation. However, if everything is strictly executed according to codes, it becomes difficult to be held liable.

Moreover, during construction and later operation and maintenance, designing in compliance with codes can prevent major safety hazards. Electrical engineering inherently carries certain risks, which we electrical professionals are well aware of. Strict adherence to codes and standards in design and construction also reduces the need for later modifications. As we all know, any modification significantly increases design and construction costs. Standardized operations can effectively control costs while avoiding project delays.

Code compliance is also crucial for ensuring engineering quality. Fully adhering to standards at least guarantees that minimum quality requirements are met. This is the essence of the importance of codes and standards.

Next, let’s introduce the main organizations responsible for establishing electrical codes in North America. First is the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) in the United States.

说话人3: 00:15:25 - 00:16:07

It has established numerous industry standards, but these standards are not mandatory and fall under performance requirements (Performance Standard). However, once these standards are referenced by building codes or electrical codes, they become mandatory.

ISO covers a wide range of standards, but those related to building electrical or general electrical design are relatively few. In contrast, NFPA standards are more specific.

说话人3: 00:16:07 - 00:19:06

ISO covers a wide range of standards, but those related to building electrical or general electrical design are relatively few. In contrast, NFPA standards are more specific.

说话人3: 00:16:07 - 00:19:06

The Fire Protection Committee in the United States has established numerous fire-related codes and standards, making it a relatively important organization. Additionally, the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) has developed many mandatory national standards, equivalent to the country’s national standards.

Another key organization is the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE), whose standards are primarily applied in the air conditioning, refrigeration, and energy efficiency sectors, mainly involving HVAC fields. Currently, North America has also adopted many energy efficiency standards in the electrical engineering field, with several developed by ASHRAE, and these standards are gradually being incorporated into building codes.

Two other organizations, TIA and EIA, primarily develop standards related to communications. These standards are typically mandatory when communication systems have high requirements; otherwise, they are similar to IEEE standards.

Another standard, UL, mainly pertains to product standards. In the U.S., equipment imported from abroad often requires NCE or UL certification to ensure compliance with national standards. These products include electrical equipment, fire alarm systems, or lighting devices. In Canada, the corresponding certifications are CSA and ULC.

Furthermore, FM certification is common in the fire protection sector. For example, fire alarm systems (such as FARM systems) often require FM certification. This certification is primarily for insurance purposes, as property insurance typically mandates that fire alarm systems have this certification. Therefore, in North America, fire alarm products usually carry FARM certification.

The above are the main organizations responsible for developing codes and standards in the United States and Canada.

说话人3: 00:19:06 - 00:22:34

Canada’s building standards system is similar to that of the United States. CSA is equivalent to the U.S. ANSI, while ULC corresponds to the U.S. UL. In terms of building codes, the U.S. adopts the International Building Code (IBC), whereas Canada’s national building codes are developed by the National Research Council (NRC). Provinces adjust the national standards based on their specific conditions to form local codes. Provinces with stronger technical capabilities develop their own codes, while smaller provinces directly adopt the national standards.

In the electrical sector, Canada has utility companies such as Hydro One and BC Hydro. The Electrical Safety Authority is responsible for the approval of electrical equipment and the review of design drawings, which differs from the power authorities in charge of transmission.

Cities are responsible for issuing development permits and building permits. Applicants must submit drawings, and construction can only begin after obtaining the permits. Final inspections are conducted by safety authorities, covering safety-related disciplines such as electrical, plumbing, natural gas, and boilers. This means permit approval and final inspections are handled by different departments.

Canada’s standards system largely follows U.S. standards but retains some unique national characteristics. As a result, the design processes in the U.S. and Canada are fundamentally similar, with only minor differences in the application and implementation of certain codes. The following section will introduce the specific standards in North America.

说话人3: 00:22:34 - 00:25:26

说话人3: 00:22:34 - 00:25:26

Some of the regulations and standards related to our electrical field. In the United States, the primary building code is the International Building Code (IBC 2024), whose main purpose is fire safety, while also covering aspects such as energy efficiency, environmental concerns, and drinking water. This code centers on safety and health.

The sections directly relevant to our electrical profession include fire alarm systems, emergency power systems, emergency lighting systems, as well as systems coordinated with elevators, smoke control systems, and access control.

In the U.S., the most important electrical code is the National Electrical Code (NFPA 70 2023), which sets the standards for electrical design and installation. Additionally, the NFPA 72 Fire Alarm Code (2025 edition) specifically addresses fire alarm systems, while NFPA 110 regulates the design and installation of emergency power systems.

NFPA 70E is a safety standard for electrical hazards, primarily targeting public spaces. It outlines requirements for preventing electric shock, including protective measures against hazards such as arc flash. This standard is not a design or installation code but rather specifies safety requirements for completed electrical systems.

Finally, NFPA 780 is the lightning protection standard. Beyond those mentioned, the NFPA has many other codes relevant to our electrical profession.

说话人3: 00:25:26 - 00:28:50

Finally, NFPA 780 is the lightning protection standard. Beyond those mentioned, the NFPA has many other codes relevant to our electrical profession.

说话人3: 00:25:26 - 00:28:50

NFPA 1 is the Fire Code. In overseas projects, NFPA 101 serves as the fire protection code for design and construction. NFPA 3 is not merely a fire alarm system standard but a commissioning standard covering the entire fire protection system, including subsystems such as fire alarm systems, sprinkler systems, elevators, and smoke control systems. NFPA 4 is a mandatory standard for integrated testing of fire alarm systems with other building fire protection systems, with the U.S. and Canada requiring implementation every 5 and 15 years, respectively, to ensure system functionality.

NFPA 13 is the sprinkler system design standard. Although it falls under fire protection water supply, it is closely related to electrical engineering. The coordination or monitoring functions of sprinkler systems must integrate with fire alarm systems, and their design depends on building type and scale to determine whether specific protection schemes are required. NFPA 20 is a critical standard for fire pumps, specifying power supply methods and connection requirements between fire alarm systems and pump control systems, which differ significantly from domestic standards. NFPA 25 addresses the commissioning and testing of sprinkler systems. Additionally, electrical professionals must also consider other relevant standards such as NFPA 90A.

说话人3: 00:28:50 - 00:29:47

The NFPA-90A Standard covers the installation requirements for air conditioning systems, including the location and specifications for smoke detectors (Dark Smoke Detectors) within air ducts.

说话人3: 00:28:50 - 00:29:47

The NFPA-90A Standard covers the installation requirements for air conditioning systems, including the location and specifications for smoke detectors (Dark Smoke Detectors) within air ducts.

The NFPA-92 Standard is formulated for smoke control systems. If the project includes a commercial kitchen, such as those equipped with stoves or similar appliances, compliance with the NFPA-96 Standard is required, which has coordination requirements with fire alarm systems.

NFPA-99 applies to hospital-type construction projects. NFPA-101 is the primary life safety code. Additionally, standards such as ASME A17.1 and CSA B44 must also be referenced.

说话人3: 00:29:48 - 00:32:42

NFPA-99 applies to hospital-type construction projects. NFPA-101 is the primary life safety code. Additionally, standards such as ASME A17.1 and CSA B44 must also be referenced.

说话人3: 00:29:48 - 00:32:42

This pertains to the design and installation codes for elevators and escalators, where the standards in the United States and Canada are largely aligned. Elevator safety requirements cover multiple aspects, including not only power supply and lighting but also specific provisions for fire alarm systems, such as meeting particular criteria at the top and bottom of elevator shafts. Additionally, fire emergency power systems must synchronize with elevator controllers during automatic switching, all of which are governed by relevant standards.

ANSI/ASHRAE/IES Standard 90.1 is a prominent building energy efficiency standard in North America in recent years, encompassing plumbing and electrical disciplines. The electrical section primarily specifies lighting and power usage standards, such as clear limits on lighting power density per square meter for different building types.

IESNA Lighting Standards are not mandatory codes but provide recommended illuminance values for various building types, projects, and zones.

ANSI/TIA/EIA-568 and 569 are communication standards that respectively define the routing methods for communication cables within buildings and the installation requirements for conduit and cable trays. Furthermore, the standards specify detailed requirements for Communication Rooms, including air conditioning, access control, ventilation, temperature control, and cable routing regulations.

The final section addresses relevant Canadian standards and codes.

说话人3: 00:32:43 - 00:34:43

The final section addresses relevant Canadian standards and codes.

说话人3: 00:32:43 - 00:34:43

First, Canada has the National Building Code and National Electrical Code. Additionally, there are fire alarm systems and their related standards.

The ULC Fire Alarm Standards are a series of regulations covering installation, commissioning, and specific requirements for various components. The three most important standards are:
- CAN/ULC-S524-2024 (Installation and Design Standard)
- CAN/ULC-S536-2024 (System Integration Testing Standard)
- CAN/ULC-S537-2019 (Verification Standard After Project Completion)

CSA-C282 focuses on the design and installation of emergency power systems. CSA-Z32 is specifically for electrical safety standards in special buildings like hospitals. CAN/ULC-1001 stipulates the testing requirements for fire alarm systems every five years.

The standard systems in the U.S. and Canada are largely aligned but differ in naming conventions. Generally, U.S. standards are more comprehensive, and many Canadian standards directly adopt U.S. regulations, such as those for fire sprinkler systems, communication systems, and energy efficiency standards. Furthermore, Canada has also adopted the Arc Flash Protection Standard (ARC Flash).

说话人3: 00:34:43 - 00:35:47

During the design and construction phases, electrical safety may not be the primary consideration. However, it is imperative to ensure that electrical equipment does not endanger surrounding personnel in the event of a short circuit once the project is completed or the building is put into use. This is precisely what CSA Z462 Standard and IEEE 1584 Guide address.

Regarding arc flash protection requirements, I wonder if any of you have encountered such demands from clients in your projects. As previously mentioned, the standards for electrical equipment in elevators and escalators are essentially identical in the U.S. and Canada, differing only in name. Additionally, CAN/CSA-B72 pertains to lightning protection systems. The aforementioned standards are national codes, with nearly identical requirements in both the U.S. and Canada.

说话人3: 00:35:47 - 00:38:10

In addition to national standards, Canadian provinces have established their own building codes and electrical codes, which are modified based on the national building and electrical codes. Furthermore, cities have developed specific regulations according to local conditions, known as City Bylaws. If projects are not conducted in North America, these local regulations may be less relevant, with the primary focus being on the aforementioned national standards.

During project implementation, coordination with local power and communication authorities is also required, such as for service entrance methods. These Utility Companies have their own codes and standards, which must be strictly adhered to.

Beyond the above standards, the HWE system encompasses a wide range of standards relevant to our work, which will be detailed later. Additionally, there are other industrial standards applicable to specific sectors. For example, North America primarily adopts HWE standards, while regions like Europe and China generally follow International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards. The American Petroleum Institute (API) standards apply to the petroleum industry, and ISA standards are specific to control equipment. The MG standards mainly pertain to motor manufacturing in North America and are production-oriented rather than design and construction standards. The NEMA (National Electrical Manufacturers Association) standards specify design and construction requirements for electrical equipment, including enclosure suitability for various environments (e.g., dry locations, outdoors, damp, or dust-proof). These standards will be explained in detail next.

说话人3: 00:38:11 - 00:39:29

说话人3: 00:38:11 - 00:39:29

Among these codes and standards, which ones are mandatory and must be complied with? This includes building codes, electrical codes, fire protection codes, standards and regulations for fire alarm systems, as well as safety-related requirements such as ArcFlash protection requirements. Among them, CSA-Z462 and NEC 70E are essentially the same content, just referred to differently in the US and Canada.

When working on local projects in North America, City bylaws must also be followed. Additionally, the AHJ (Authority Having Jurisdiction), which can be agencies like the fire department or electrical authority, is responsible for building approvals, permit approvals, development approvals, and inspections.

All these codes primarily address safety requirements, including fire safety and structural safety, among others.

说话人1: 00:39:29 - 00:39:38

In addition, it also includes standards related to health and safety.

说话人3: 00:39:38 - 00:41:18

All these codes primarily address safety requirements, including fire safety and structural safety, among others.

说话人1: 00:39:29 - 00:39:38

In addition, it also includes standards related to health and safety.

说话人3: 00:39:38 - 00:41:18

We refer to this as performance standards, which are not mandatory. These standards represent certain technical performance requirements in the design process—indicators that need to be achieved from a technical standpoint. Such standards serve as guidelines, including industrial standards, design manuals, and conventional practices during construction or design.

We call this good practice, meaning proven feasible approaches based on experience. While not compulsory, it is advisable to meet these standards. IEEE provides detailed specifications for this, which we refer to as the Color Book, and this will be further explained in subsequent courses.

In North America, different codes apply to manufacturing versus design and construction. For example, in Canada, when manufacturing equipment such as switchgear, manufacturers follow Part One of the National Electrical Code, which guides design and construction, while Part Two applies to standards during the production process. These two parts are largely similar but also have some specific differences.

Next, we will discuss the practical application of these codes and standards.

说话人3: 00:41:19 - 00:42:42

First, we need to understand these codes and standards and know how to obtain them. As Dean Zhu mentioned, China Construction Eighth Engineering Division (CSCEC8D) is currently building a codes and standards database. These codes can be downloaded from the official websites of relevant institutions, but usually require payment. In Canada, some building codes are free, but the Electrical Code and other standards still need to be purchased.

For professionals engaged in electrical design and construction, mastering these codes is crucial. Designers must be thoroughly familiar with the codes, while construction personnel can follow the drawings without necessarily needing in-depth knowledge of all codes. However, they still require some understanding of construction-related aspects not covered in the design.

Our clients only need a basic awareness of these codes, but if they can acquire more knowledge, it will facilitate project development and evaluation work. These codes and standards hold significant importance in the industry.

说话人3: 00:42:42 - 00:43:47

When discussing the roles of different stakeholders, we can analogize standards and norms-setting organizations to legislative bodies like Congress. The enforcement departments, on the other hand, resemble courts or government agencies responsible for law enforcement.

During the design process, out of consideration for the client, we often need to advocate for them at the level of applying norms and standards since they are the ones paying the fees. This is similar to how lawyers defend their clients in court. The client is equivalent to the party who hires the attorney, while the design and construction teams play the role of the lawyers.

说话人3: 00:43:47 - 00:46:01

In North America, building codes are typically updated every five to six years, while other codes are revised every three years. For large-scale projects, their construction timelines may span across code update cycles. To address this issue, code implementations usually include a transition period. For example, codes published in 2024 often do not become officially effective until 2025, when they are formally adopted by state, provincial, or municipal safety authorities. This transition period typically lasts six to twelve months to allow for discussion and feedback from stakeholders.

For projects already in the construction phase, if the new code has not yet taken effect during the design phase or when applying for building or electrical permits, the project will continue to comply with the original code, including during construction and final inspection. However, if the project is still in the design phase or the relevant permits have not been approved when the new code becomes effective, it must adhere to the new code requirements. This mechanism ensures a smooth transition during code updates.

说话人3: 00:46:02 - 00:48:53

说话人3: 00:46:02 - 00:48:53

In North America, including the United States and Canada, many clients import electrical equipment from Asia or other countries to reduce costs. However, both the U.S. and Canada mandate that imported equipment must comply with local certification standards. The U.S. has its own certification system, while Canada has its separate requirements. Certification can be conducted either after the equipment arrives or completed before export. The best approach is to obtain certification prior to export to avoid subsequent complications and additional expenses. Local certification is not only costly but also carries the risk of failure. We have extensive experience in this area.

For projects involving equipment imports from China or other countries, it is crucial to understand the specific certification requirements of the target country in advance to prevent project delays or cost overruns. Typically, certification between the U.S. and Canada is relatively straightforward, but equipment imported from Europe or Asia requires recertification by local authorities—a process that is cumbersome, time-consuming, expensive, and carries approval risks. Therefore, special attention must be paid to this issue when operating projects in other countries.

Additionally, North America’s electrical systems differ from China’s, such as operating at 60 Hz instead of the domestic 50 Hz. Parameters like voltage must also meet local standards. These are all technical considerations to keep in mind.

说话人3: 00:48:55 - 00:50:37

说话人3: 00:48:55 - 00:50:37

These regulations must be strictly enforced, but there are exceptions, which we refer to as “variance.” Typically, when on-site implementation of the regulations is not feasible, a variance can be applied for.

The application must be accompanied by a written explanation from a qualified institution or individual, such as the Design Management Institute. The competent authority is responsible for reviewing variance applications, which require the submission of relevant written materials, including completed forms or formal letters, signed and stamped. The review outcome may be either approved or denied.

Generally, variances are only approved when on-site implementation is unfeasible and does not pose significant risks to safety or other aspects. We have some experience in such projects and usually do not recommend modifying the regulations lightly unless the cost of full compliance is prohibitively high. In such cases, we can assist in handling the process.

These exceptions must be submitted by the Design Management Institute and approved by the competent authority.

说话人3: 00:50:38 - 00:53:12

During the construction process, if non-compliant situations arise, although the design phase has typically undergone review, violations identified during construction will prompt authorities (e.g., State/Provincial Safety Authority) to issue work stoppage orders. Hence, both design and construction phases must prioritize regulatory compliance.

With six years of experience in building electrical design in China, I previously worked at Northeast Design Institute. The current industry environment differs from our era—back then, regulatory adherence was less stringent, and not every code required strict enforcement. Domestic mechanisms were also incomplete, lacking systematic design review processes and final inspection procedures. Compared to international standards, Chinese codes exhibit gaps in granularity, with some project metrics ambiguously defined, leading designers, contractors, and inspectors to often adopt a “barely compliant” approach.

Later, I will explore balancing project costs, timelines, and construction safety. Over-pursuing excessive standards (e.g., far exceeding code requirements) inevitably escalates costs, conflicting with developers’ or contractors’ goals of cost control and schedule compression. Thus, scientific coordination of these critical factors is essential during design.

说话人3: 00:53:13 - 00:56:26

说话人3: 00:53:13 - 00:56:26

In terms of code application, we have encountered some confusion or made mistakes in the past. When working on large-scale projects, it is common to hire specialized code consultants. These consultants are primarily experts in building codes, particularly complex regulations involving multiple disciplines such as fire safety codes. Their responsibilities include providing code review reports for large projects to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements, though their fees are relatively high.

Without code consultants, we need to regularly update our knowledge of codes and understand the latest regulatory requirements and their interrelationships. Currently, we are conducting training on the latest codes, with a focus on explaining the relationships between different codes.

In North America, large-scale projects typically employ code consultants. To my knowledge, China does not yet have specialized design institutes for this purpose, though there is a drawing review mechanism—it’s unclear whether this includes code reviews. Additionally, attention must be paid to local special requirements, and it is important to maintain contact with local municipal or safety management authorities to stay updated on new regulations published on their websites.

When large companies undertake design work, they often hire third-party design institutes for drawing joint reviews to avoid design errors or omissions. During the design and installation construction process, quality control is particularly crucial to prevent project losses or delays. It’s important to note that code requirements may vary across different countries, regions, and even within different areas of the same country.

说话人3: 00:56:26 - 01:00:37

说话人3: 00:56:26 - 01:00:37

There are differences between regulatory and standard requirements. Taking North America and China as examples, North American regulations are more detailed and specific. In the application of battery standards, China’s domestic standards initially involve three types of verification calculations, each with significant differences in power supply methods compared to those in the U.S. and Canada.

The IPWE standard also differs greatly from the IEC standards of the International Electrotechnical Commission, including aspects such as fire pump activation and monitoring signals. There are also variations between U.S. and Canadian standards, with the U.S. regulations being more comprehensive and stringent, particularly in leading the way in energy efficiency. While Canadian and U.S. battery standards are generally similar, differences remain in areas such as ATS application and fire alarm requirements. Even within Canada and the U.S., provincial requirements vary—for instance, Ontario places greater emphasis on fire safety, while British Columbia prioritizes energy efficiency.

China’s regulatory design, construction, and implementation processes are highly stringent, with each step requiring compliance before proceeding.
